question_text:
Text 1
Historians of English have long noted that in the northern districts settled by Norse speakers in the ninth and tenth centuries, noun endings wore away sooner than they did in the south. The explanation lies with adult learners. People who pick up a language after childhood rarely master its case endings, and the streamlined version they speak is what their children hear. The Norse settlers, who needed English to farm, trade, and marry among their neighbors, were such learners, and the district records show the loss beginning where settler households were thickest.

Text 2
Few linguists doubt that adult learners streamline a language's endings, and the northern pattern is consistent with that process. It may be, though, that the learners who mattered most were not the settlers. English-speaking farmers in those districts dealt daily with Norse-speaking landlords and merchants, and many may have learned enough Norse to bargain in it, then carried the shortened habits back into their own English. On one reading, settler households would show the change no earlier than the English-speaking households around them, a pattern the surviving district records do not rule out.

Based on the texts, how do the authors of Text 1 and Text 2 differ in their treatment of the northern loss of noun endings?
answer_a: Both texts attribute the loss to adult learners, but Text 1 places those learners among the Norse-speaking settlers, whereas Text 2 raises the possibility that they were English speakers who had learned Norse.
answer_b: Text 1 presents adult learning as the cause of the northern loss, whereas Text 2 suggests that the loss may have had a different source than adult learning.
answer_c: Text 1 holds that the loss began among English speakers who had learned Norse, whereas Text 2 holds that it began among settlers who had learned English.
answer_d: Text 1 attributes the loss to adult learners generally, whereas Text 2 maintains that the settlers' households played no part in the change in the northern districts.
explanation: Choice A is the best answer. Both texts accept that adult learners streamline a language's endings: Text 1 states this as the explanation, and Text 2 says that few linguists doubt it and that the northern pattern is consistent with it. The texts part ways on a second point, which community's learners mattered. Text 1 identifies the Norse-speaking settlers, who needed English, as the learners. Text 2 suggests, with the hedge 'may,' that English-speaking farmers who learned some Norse may have been the ones who carried shortened habits into English.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect. It places the disagreement on the shared assumption. Text 2 explicitly accepts that adult learners streamline endings and calls the northern pattern consistent with that process; what it questions is who the learners were.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. It reverses which author holds which view. Text 1, not Text 2, identifies the Norse-speaking settlers learning English as the source of the loss, and Text 2 only raises the possibility that English speakers who learned Norse were involved.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. It inflates Text 2's hedged claim. Text 2 says only that settler households may have changed no earlier than their English-speaking neighbors, not that the settlers played no part, and it does not reject adult learning as the cause.

question_text:
Text 1
A thick earthen wall soaks up the day's heat and returns it slowly, so the room behind it reaches its warmest point hours after the outdoors does and never matches the outdoor high. In the dry highland town where one builder recorded this pattern, evenings turn sharply cool, and the stored heat drains from the wall before dawn, leaving it ready to absorb the next day's warmth. The builder concludes that dense walls keep rooms comfortable wherever summers are hot, and that choosing the right wall thickness matters far more than local climate.

Text 2
Sensors placed in earthen houses in a humid harbor town recorded an interior peak that arrived well after the outdoor peak and stayed several degrees below it. Yet nights there cool by only a degree or two, and by midnight the walls were often warmer than the air outside. One reading is that a wall may give up its heat only to air cooler than itself, in which case a wall unable to unload overnight could begin each morning partly loaded. If so, the comfort that thick walls provide may owe less to thickness than to how far temperatures fall after sunset.

Based on the texts, which claim from Text 1 would the author of Text 2 most likely still accept?
answer_a: Heat stored in a wall drains away most fully on evenings that stay warm.
answer_b: A wall can release stored heat only into air that is cooler than the wall.
answer_c: The room behind a thick earthen wall reaches its warmest point later than the outdoors does.
answer_d: Dense earthen walls keep rooms comfortable in any region where summers are hot.
explanation: Choice C is the best answer because it is a claim Text 1 makes (the room behind a thick earthen wall "reaches its warmest point hours after the outdoors does") that does not depend on the condition Text 2 questions. Text 2's own sensors in the harbor town found an interior peak that "arrived well after the outdoor peak," so the delayed peak held even where nights stay warm. Text 2's hedged reading concerns only whether the wall can unload its heat overnight, which bears on Text 1's conclusion about comfort, not on the timing of the peak.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. Text 1 says that stored heat drains from the wall before dawn, but only in a town where evenings turn sharply cool; it never says draining is most complete on warm evenings. That would reverse the condition Text 2 raises, since Text 2 suggests a wall unloads less, not more, when nights stay warm.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect. This is the possibility Text 2 raises when it suggests a wall may give up heat only to cooler air, so Text 2's author might well accept it, but Text 1 never makes this claim. Text 1 simply says the heat drains away each night and does not state what the outside air must be like for that to happen.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. Text 1 concludes that dense walls keep rooms comfortable wherever summers are hot, but Text 2 suggests that comfort may depend on how far temperatures fall after sunset. Text 2 reports a lower and later interior peak yet still questions whether comfort follows in a place where nights stay warm, so its author would not accept this broad claim.
